tldr: De Morlhon presents Docker's sandbox platform for coding agents (microVMs with filesystem and network control, shareable Kits, cloud sandboxes) and the internal 'AI factory' Docker built on it.
summary: Jean-Laurent de Morlhon frames the talk around four questions: can you trust an agent, repeat its setup, run it without you, and build on it? Each agent runs in its own microVM with its own kernel and a Docker daemon, isolated by hardware virtualisation (Intel VT-x, AMD-V). A filesystem manager mounts only chosen directories, and a network proxy enforces policies and injects credentials on outbound calls, so the agent only sees a dummy value. A demo shows the sbx CLI blocking a disallowed site. Docker Kits package a Dockerfile with a kit.yaml of sandbox policies in one OCI image; Docker plans to donate the new spec to the CNCF.

The same sandboxes run in Docker's cloud (sbx move hands a local session over), behind an MCP gateway that can allow individual tools of a server, with a web UI, an OpenAPI API and a TypeScript SDK. Since February Docker has run an internal 'AI factory' on top: agents co-write a design document with humans, a PM agent splits it into Jira tickets, an orchestrator runs four or five implementer agents in parallel, review agents check each PR, and a human is pinged in Slack to approve. Most human time goes into commenting on design documents; reviewing 10,000-line PRs remains a problem.
keyPoints: Credentials never enter the sandbox: the network proxy swaps a placeholder for the real API key or SSH credential on outbound calls, limiting the damage from info-stealing packages.
MicroVM isolation is hardware-enforced and boots fast enough to run 6-20 agents side by side on a laptop.
Docker Kits bundle the sandbox image and its policy (allowed hosts, injected secrets, capabilities) under one OCI digest so a team can share the exact agent setup.
The MCP gateway can allow specific tools within an MCP server, for example read but not destructive write operations.
In Docker's internal factory the human effort shifts to design review; implementation is parallelised across sandboxed agents and the output is tracked as artifacts rather than sessions.
takeaways: Stop giving agents broad GitHub tokens or raw API keys; run them in a sandbox that injects scoped credentials at the network layer.
Write down network and filesystem policies for your agents and share them as a versioned image, not as personal setup steps.
Try the free sbx CLI to run a coding agent in a microVM on your laptop.

quotes.text: I think the real power of sandboxes is that it's more like a seatbelt in your car.

watchIf: You let coding agents run with real credentials on your machine and want a quick look at how Docker isolates them and orchestrates many in parallel.
